There is a cathedral in the center of Amsterdam that has been converted into a conference venue. You can rent it for corporate events, art exhibitions, and private parties. There is a church in London that is now a nightclub. Another in Dublin that houses a restaurant. Across Western Europe, the great physical monuments of Christendom are being repurposed, not because the buildings have failed but because the civilization they represented has moved on.

This is not a story about buildings. It is a story about the end of an arrangement that shaped Western civilization for a millennium and a half, an arrangement so pervasive that most people who lived within it could not see its edges. For fifteen centuries, to be European was to be Christian, to be Christian was to be civilized, and to be civilized was to belong to a world ordered by Christian assumptions about God, time, morality, law, art, sex, death, and meaning. That world, called Christendom, is dying. And the death, depending on where you stand, is either the greatest catastrophe in the history of the faith or its greatest opportunity.

What Christendom Was

Christendom is not a synonym for Christianity. Christianity is a faith, a set of convictions about who God is and what God has done. Christendom is a political and cultural arrangement in which that faith becomes the organizing principle of an entire civilization, fused with state power, embedded in law, assumed in education, and enforced, where necessary, by coercion.

I pastor a church in a country that has not gotten that far yet, and I say yet on purpose. The church keeps getting one thing wrong about the funeral. Christendom is not Christianity. One is a faith. The numbers are no longer debatable. In 1999, Gallup found that 70 percent of Americans belonged to a church, synagogue, or mosque. By 2020, that number had fallen to 47 percent, the first time in the history of the poll that it dropped below the majority line. By 2023, it had settled at 45 percent. In a single generation, the United States went from being a nation where church membership was a default social behavior to one where it is a minority practice.

Pew Research Center's Religious Landscape Study tells the same story from a different angle. In 2007, 78 percent of Americans identified as Christian. By 2021, that number had fallen to 63 percent, and projections suggest it could drop below 50 percent by the mid-2040s. The decline is not concentrated among any single demographic. It is happening among whites and people of color, among the college-educated and those without degrees, in rural areas and urban centers. It is, by any sociological measure, a broad-based cultural shift.

And yet the dominant response from church leadership has been a combination of denial, blame, and strategic tinkering, as if the problem were a matter of better marketing, younger worship leaders, or more compelling sermon series. The institutional church, by and large, has refused to sit with the most uncomfortable possibility: that people are leaving not because they misunderstand the church, but because they understand it all too well.

The statistics have been recited so often that they have acquired the quality of liturgy. Roughly 60 to 65 percent of young adults who were regular churchgoers in their teens disengage from church life by their mid-twenties. The decline in religious affiliation among 18-to-35-year-olds has been steeper and faster than in any other age cohort. Only about 30 percent of millennials and an even smaller percentage of Gen Z say they attend religious services regularly. The church is aging, graying, and shrinking, and the generation that should be replenishing its ranks is, with remarkable consistency, choosing not to.

The church's response to these statistics has been, for the most part, a case study in misdiagnosis. Assuming that the problem is one of presentation rather than substance, churches across America have invested heavily in aesthetic and experiential upgrades designed to make the church more attractive to young adults. Better coffee. Fog machines. LED light shows. Worship bands that sound like Coldplay. Sermon series with cinematic title sequences. Apps for everything. Pastors in skinny jeans. The operating assumption is that young adults are consumers who will attend church if the product is sufficiently polished, and that the church's competitive disadvantage is one of production values rather than credibility.

He described Jesus as a cage fighter, an alpha male, a warrior who would return at the end of days to deliver divine violence. The message was clear: godly manhood was aggressive, confrontational, and unapologetically dominant. Anything else was weakness. Anything else was feminization. Anything else was failure.

Driscoll was not an outlier. He was the loudest voice in a movement that had been building for decades, a movement that defined masculinity in terms of power, authority, and control, and that located these qualities at the center of God's design for men. John Eldredge's Wild at Heart, published in 2001 and eventually selling over four million copies, told men that they were designed to be warriors, adventurers, and rescuers, and that the modern church, with its emphasis on gentleness, servanthood, and emotional vulnerability, had stolen their masculine identity. The result was a theology of masculinity that bore almost no resemblance to the man at the center of the Christian story. In 1968, Thomas Merton (Trappist monk, contemplative writer, and one of the most influential spiritual voices of the twentieth century) traveled to Asia to meet with Buddhist monks and teachers. In Bangkok, he delivered a lecture to a conference of monastics. He spoke of the convergences between Christian and Buddhist contemplative practice, the shared commitment to silence, simplicity, and the disciplined emptying of the self. He spoke of what Christians could learn from Buddhism without abandoning their own tradition. Later that day, Merton died, electrocuted by a faulty fan in his hotel room, in circumstances that remain somewhat mysterious. He was fifty-three years old.

Merton's Asian journey was not a departure from his Christian faith. It was a deepening of it. He had spent twenty-seven years in a Trappist monastery, living under a rule of silence, prayer, and manual labor. He had written over sixty books on Christian spirituality, theology, and contemplative practice. He was, by any measure, one of the most deeply rooted Christians of his century. And it was precisely the depth of his rootedness that gave him the freedom to engage Buddhism without fear, to recognize in another tradition the same realities he had encountered in his own, expressed in different language and practiced through different forms.

Merton's example points to a truth that the Western church has been slow to grasp: Christianity and Buddhism, despite their profound metaphysical differences, share a remarkable convergence in their contemplative practices, their diagnosis of the human condition, and their prescriptions for spiritual transformation. The church that dismisses Buddhism as a pagan philosophy or an incompatible worldview is not protecting its faith. It is impoverishing it.

In January 1525, a small group of men gathered in the home of Felix Manz in Zurich. They had been followers of Ulrich Zwingli, the city's reformer, but had grown convinced that Zwingli's reformation had not gone far enough. Zwingli had broken with Rome, but he had not broken with the fundamental assumption that had governed Christianity since Constantine: that the church and the state were bound together, that every citizen was a church member, and that infant baptism was the rite of entry into both civic and spiritual life.

That evening, Conrad Grebel baptized George Blaurock, an adult who had already been baptized as an infant. It was an act of profound theological significance and extraordinary political danger. By rebaptizing an adult, these men were not merely making a statement about the proper subjects of baptism. They were rejecting the entire Christendom model. They were saying that the church was not a territorial institution coextensive with the state but a voluntary community of committed believers. They were saying that faith could not be inherited, imposed, or assumed, it had to be chosen.

For this, they would be hunted, imprisoned, tortured, and killed, not only by Catholics, but by the very Protestants whose reformation they believed they were completing.

The average American will spend roughly 90,000 hours at work over the course of a lifetime. For the Christian who takes vocation seriously, this is not a neutral fact. It is a theological one. The majority of your waking life is spent in a context where your faith is, at best, irrelevant to the people around you and, at worst, a source of suspicion. The question of how to be a Christian at work is not a peripheral concern. It is one of the central questions of the integrated life.

And the church has been remarkably unhelpful in answering it. The dominant models on offer are, roughly, two. The first is the "workplace evangelism" model, which treats the office as a mission field and your coworkers as potential converts. This model produces the person who leaves tracts in the break room, invites colleagues to church every Monday, and manages to reference Jesus in every performance review. The second is the "sacred-secular divide" model, which treats work as a necessary evil, the thing you endure in order to fund the things that actually matter: church, family, ministry. In this model, your work has no intrinsic spiritual significance. It is simply how you pay the bills.

Both models are failures. The first makes you insufferable. The second makes your faith irrelevant. Neither takes seriously the theological claim that lies at the heart of Christian vocation: that all of human life (including the hours spent in meetings, spreadsheets, patient care, construction, teaching, and code) is lived before God and can be lived for God. The integrated life refuses both errors. It insists that the God who cares about your prayer life cares equally about your professional life, and that the two are not separate compartments but a single existence lived under a single lordship.
